analysis.one_liner: Freezes all new endangered species listings and critical habitat designations until Congress reauthorizes the Endangered Species Act.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have frozen every new endangered species protection, was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee with 53 cosponsors and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Endangered Species Act to bar the Interior Secretary from listing any new species as endangered or threatened, or designating any critical habitat, until Congress reauthorizes the Act with new funding authority. Because the freeze would last until that reauthorization happened, it could stop new species protections indefinitely. In effect, it would trade wildlife protections for relief from land-use restrictions that listings and habitat designations impose on landowners and resource businesses.
analysis.who_benefits: Land developers, timber, mining, oil and gas, and agricultural operators whose land or operations could be restricted by new species listings or critical habitat designations. A freeze on all new listings would remove that regulatory risk without waiting for case-by-case reform of the Act.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would prohibit the Interior Secretary from determining that any species is endangered or threatened, so no new species would gain ESA protections while the freeze is in place.
It would also block all new critical habitat designations, which are the part of the Act that most directly limits how private and public land can be used.

The freeze would run until the first fiscal year for which Congress specifically authorizes appropriations under the Act — in other words, until the Act is reauthorized — giving land users relief from new restrictions without any need for a targeted fix.

analysis.who_pays: Wildlife and the ecosystems they depend on, and by extension the public. Species sliding toward extinction would get no protection during the freeze, and extinction is permanent. The Endangered Species Act exists to preserve species for the general public, so suspending new listings suspends a public good indefinitely if reauthorization never comes.

drawbacks.text: The moratorium would leave imperiled species with no path to protection: a species that qualified as endangered during the freeze would simply get nothing, and if it went extinct while waiting, the loss could not be undone.
Blocking critical habitat designations removes the tool that protects the land a species actually needs to survive, not just the species on paper.
The bill pairs no reform with the freeze — it simply shuts down new listings until reauthorization, which the bill does not require or schedule, so the freeze could last indefinitely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered landowners and resource industries freedom from new restrictions, but it achieved that by suspending the main mechanism that prevents extinctions, with no time limit and no alternative safeguard. Delays in listing are not cost-free: species that deteriorate past the point of recovery are lost permanently, and that loss falls on everyone, not on the industries that would gain from the freeze. Whatever the merits of reauthorizing and updating the Act, a blanket indefinite freeze was a blunt way to get there.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Bonilla of Texas introduced the bill on January 19, 1995, joined by 24 original cosponsors, nearly all Texas Republicans along with a few Texas Democrats.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Resources, the committee with jurisdiction over the Endangered Species Act.
On January 23, 1995, the committee requested an executive comment from the Interior Department; total cosponsorship reached 53 members, 38 Republicans and 15 Democrats.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the action history after that point, and the bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wildlife and the public, because the Endangered Species Act's listing and habitat protections kept operating. The developers and resource industries that backed the freeze gained nothing from it.

for.name: Henry Bonilla
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 19, 1995 and recruited 24 original cosponsors, nearly all from the Texas delegation.

against.name: House Committee on Resources
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; the action history shows no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled, and the bill died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship leaned heavily Republican — 38 of 53 cosponsors were Republicans, with 15 Democrats, most from Texas — but the bill never reached a vote, so the chamber's actual split was never measured.

industries.note: New endangered species listings and critical habitat designations can restrict building and land conversion, so a freeze on both removes that risk from development decisions. The public loses the habitat protections in exchange.

industries.industry: Timber, mining, and oil and gas
industries.note: Listed species and critical habitat can limit logging, mining, and drilling on both private and public land. A listing moratorium would prevent any new such limits from arising.
Species listings and habitat designations can affect grazing, water use, and pesticide practices. The freeze would shield those operations from new ESA-based restrictions.
